slides.headline: SAY THE POINT FIRST
slides.body: Why interviewers tune out by your third sentence.
Most interviewers decide whether you're worth hearing before you reach your point.

slides.headline: LEAD WITH THE ANSWER
slides.body: "Yes, I've led a team of 6." Then the story. Context goes second, not first.

slides.headline: ONE MESSAGE, ONE ASK
slides.body: Send a recruiter three questions in one email and you get one answer. Usually to the easiest one.

slides.headline: TRADE "I THINK" FOR A NUMBER
slides.body: "I helped grow sales" becomes "I grew sales 18% in 6 months." Numbers get remembered.

slides.headline: SAY BACK WHAT YOU HEARD
slides.body: Not sure what they're asking? Repeat it in one line first. It buys you time and saves you from the wrong answer.

slides.headline: DELETE YOUR LAST SENTENCE
slides.body: In cover letters and follow-ups it's usually a softer copy of your first one. Cut it, send.

slides.headline: SAVE THIS
slides.body: Read it again the night before your next interview.

caption:
Your best answer is in sentence three. Interviewers stop listening at sentence one.

Someone asks "Why should we hire you?" and most candidates start with where they went to college. The real answer, the 18% or the team of 6, shows up 40 seconds later. By then the interviewer is writing their next question.

The fix isn't better vocabulary. It's order.

Answer first, story second, one ask per message. Same rule for a recruiter email on LinkedIn, a cover letter, or the salary call.

Of all the interview tips out there, this is the one nobody teaches. Five communication skills, one week of practice each.

Save this before your next interview.
